back: Setting the price by adding a mark-up (a percentage of cost) to the cost per unit.
Mark-up (%) = profit ÷ cost × 100. Profit margin (%) = profit ÷ selling price × 100. The margin is smaller than the mark-up.
A high price at launch to earn a large profit per unit from early buyers; the price is usually lowered later.
A low price at launch to win market share quickly; the price may be raised later.
Charging different prices to different customers or at different times for the same product.
Changing the price quickly as demand, stock or rivals' prices change, common in online sales and transport.
Setting prices such as US\$4.95 instead of US\$5.00 because buyers may see them as lower.
Costs, competition, demand and customers' sensitivity to price, market conditions and the firm's objectives.
If demand is elastic a price cut raises revenue; if inelastic a price rise raises revenue.
